tldr: To eliminate wasteful trial-and-error in robotic grinding and sanding—where removing material cannot be undone—this sim-to-real platform simulates geometry and appearance changes directly on the GPU, bridging the gap to real-world calibration and perception model training.
hero_caption: RoboFin3D simulating grinding and sanding processes. The left two images capture large material removal during grinding, while the right two capture coating removal and appearance change during sanding, closely matching real-world behavior.
overview:
Surface finishing operations like grinding and sanding are vital steps in manufacturing automation. Automating them with robots, however, faces a major hurdle: material removal is irreversible. Once you make a mistake, you cannot restore the workpiece to its original state. Developing and evaluating control policies like reinforcement learning requires massive numbers of trials. Consuming a new workpiece for every run is costly and time-consuming, making reproducible experiments difficult.

To solve this, the authors built RoboFin3D, a surface finishing simulation platform on top of Isaac Sim and the Newton physics engine. The core idea is representing the workpiece's changing geometry using a signed distance field (SDF)—a volumetric representation storing distances to the object's boundary—while tracking surface changes during sanding with a separate surface field. By handling everything from contact mechanics to rendering directly on the GPU without regenerating meshes, the platform achieves fast, artifact-free simulation.

Additionally, the authors developed WeldGen, a module that automatically places weld beads on 8,918 CAD models to provide diverse simulation assets. After calibrating material removal parameters against real-world experimental data, the simulated material removal closely matches physical experiments. Furthermore, fine-tuning a segmentation model (SAM2) using synthetic images automatically generated by the simulator substantially improves the recognition of unsanded regions on real-world images.
contributions: Built a grinding and sanding simulator that handles contact computation and appearance changes by updating and rendering SDFs and surface fields directly without intermediate mesh reconstruction.
Provided 8,918 workpiece assets via WeldGen, a module that generates weld beads on CAD models from the ABC dataset with controllable task difficulty.
Calibrated simulation parameters using real-world machining data, demonstrating high simulation fidelity in both grinding removal volume and sanding pattern overlap.
Fine-tuned an image recognition model (SAM2) on automatically generated and annotated simulation images, significantly boosting segmentation performance on unsanded regions in real-world images.

sections.heading: Moving away from throwaway workpieces in robotic trials
sections.summary: Because grinding and sanding permanently remove material, physical trial-and-error is expensive and hard to reproduce. This work introduces RoboFin3D, the first integrated platform for contact, geometry change, and rendering.
sections.details:
Robotic surface finishing in manufacturing removes material with abrasive tools, irreversibly altering the workpiece on every attempt. Developing and evaluating control policies takes dozens or hundreds of trials, but worn-down workpieces cannot be restored. As a result, physical experiments incur heavy material costs, making controlled benchmark comparisons nearly impossible.

If a simulator can reset the workpiece to its initial state at any moment, researchers can run reproducible evaluations repeatedly at zero material cost. Looking at prior work, however, individual techniques have addressed contact mechanics, material removal process models, micro-topography rendering of machined surfaces, or synthetic data generation for perception. Yet none have integrated all of these into a single simulation platform. Evaluating closed-loop robot control requires real-time coupling among robot contact, the resulting changes in geometry and appearance, and camera views capturing those changes.

RoboFin3D tackles this challenge. It focuses on two processes: grinding, which cuts away large volumes like weld beads using rigid grinding wheels, and sanding, which smooths surfaces or strips paint and rust using sandpaper. By using SDFs and surface fields, it establishes an end-to-end pipeline covering contact computation, live updates, and rendering without mesh conversions.

captions.F2: Overall workflow of RoboFin3D. Welded workpieces generated by WeldGen are loaded into the simulator, and simulation parameters are calibrated against real experimental data. The resulting synthetic data trains perception models, enabling safe evaluation of control policies before real-world deployment.

sections.heading: SDF-native design for fast, accurate surface transformation
sections.summary: Combining Isaac Sim and Newton physics engine, RoboFin3D manages geometry (SDF) and appearance (surface field) in shared GPU buffers. A fully GPU-native pipeline executes contact physics through rendering without any mesh conversions.
sections.details:
RoboFin3D builds on Isaac Sim 6.1.0 and the Newton physics engine. Its architecture and individual components are designed as follows:

### II-A Automated Welded Workpiece Generation (WeldGen)
To provide diverse workpieces, the authors developed WeldGen to place weld beads onto 8,918 CAD meshes curated from the ABC dataset. It samples weld curves anywhere on a mesh and attaches bead geometry. By tuning curve length, geodesic curvature (surface bending), and exposure, users can freely adjust task difficulty. Because it retains both the original mesh and the added bead geometry as ground truth, the assets can directly generate training data for perception models.

### II-B Modeling Geometry Change in Grinding
Because grinding removes substantial material, the workpiece geometry itself must change. Workpiece geometry is tracked by a signed distance field (SDF) $\phi$, where $\phi < 0$ denotes the object interior and the zero-isosurface marks the boundary. Newton references this SDF to compute hydroelastic contact, which models compliant contact surfaces and pressure distributions. Material removal follows Preston's law (wear is proportional to contact pressure and slip velocity), where normal wear rate $r$ scales with excess pressure beyond a threshold $p_c$. Assuming constant wheel rotation speed, it is computed via an effective wear coefficient $k$ as $r = k \max(0, p - p_c)$.

### II-C Modeling Appearance Change in Sanding
Sanding primarily strips thin coatings or rust, so the workpiece geometry $\phi$ remains unchanged. Instead, a surface field $D$ tracks sanding progress. Following Preston's law as well, $D$ accumulates the time integral of contact pressure $p$ and slip velocity $v_{\mathrm{slip}}$. Given coating thickness $h_c$ and Preston coefficient $K_P$, the rate is $\dot{D} = \frac{K_P}{h_c} p v_{\mathrm{slip}}$, where $D=1$ denotes fully removed coating. Isaac Sim's RTX renderer uses a custom shader to blend the color, roughness, and metallicity between coating and substrate smoothly using $\min(D, 1)$ as the weight.

### II-D Fully GPU-Native Pipeline
Both states ($\phi$ and $D$) reside in shared GPU buffers directly accessible by CUDA and Vulkan. NVIDIA Warp updates the fields, Newton queries the SDF for contact, and custom RTX renderer shaders read the fields directly for display. Eliminating CPU transfers and costly mesh reconstructions (such as marching cubes) is the core technical strength of this system.

sections.heading: Calibrating against real machining and driving perception training
sections.summary: The authors established a procedure to calibrate contact and wear parameters using real-world machining data. They also built a pipeline to fine-tune SAM2 on synthetic training data for real-world image segmentation.
sections.details:
A simulator is of little use if it diverges from real physical behavior, no matter how fast it runs. This section presents parameter calibration using real-world data and sim-to-real transfer for perception.

### III-A Real-to-Sim Calibration
For both grinding and sanding, a physical robot executes two passes (Pass 1 and Pass 2) on workpieces. The authors use Pass 1 to tune parameters while reserving Pass 2 to evaluate predictive accuracy under a rigorous protocol. Workpiece surfaces before and after machining are scanned with high precision using a Keyence VR-6000 optical profiler.
- Grinding calibration: First, the effective wear coefficient $k$ is fit to the volume removed in Pass 1. Then, holding $k$ fixed, contact stiffness (pressure per penetration depth) and threshold pressure $p_c$ are tuned by comparing scanned cross-sections against simulated height profiles.
- Sanding calibration: The ratio $K_P / h_c$ is fit so the simulated coating removal pattern matches the substrate exposure pattern estimated from optical scans.

### III-B Sim-to-Real Perception
Automating sanding requires pinpointing unsanded regions from camera images. However, manually labeling real images at the pixel level requires massive effort. This is where simulation shines.

In simulation, pixels where appearance field $D$ changed relative to the initial state are labeled as sanded, while unchanged pixels are labeled as unsanded, automatically producing clean ground-truth masks. Using these synthetic images, the authors fine-tune SAM2 (Tiny). The pretrained image encoder is frozen, training only the prompt encoder and mask decoder. During inference, providing the overall workpiece bounding box as a prompt reliably predicts the unsanded mask.

sections.heading: Evaluating simulation fidelity and real-world perception accuracy
sections.summary: The calibrated simulation accurately reproduced real-world removal volumes and exposure patterns. Furthermore, SAM2 trained purely on synthetic images raised unsanded region IoU on real test images from 77.15% to 84.47%, reaching 97.41% when paired with limited real images.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated both the physical fidelity of the simulation and the performance of perception models trained on synthetic images.

### IV-A Simulation Fidelity Evaluation
Both real-world and simulated machining ran under admittance control targeting a 15 N normal force. Simulation Pass 2 resumed directly from the geometry ground down in Pass 1.

In grinding, the simulation faithfully reproduced physical behavior: the rounded bead top flattened into a plateau in Pass 1 and ground down further in Pass 2 (Figure F4). Looking at cumulative removed volume errors (TABLE I), simulated material removal matched physical measurements closely.

In sanding, fully cleared regions ($D \ge 1$) were compared against substrate exposure regions estimated from optical scans. The overlap measured an IoU of 0.81 in Pass 1 and 0.89 in Pass 2. Although the simulation tended to overestimate exposed area by 11.2% to 16.5% compared to the physical trial, the spreading wear pattern was captured remarkably well.

### IV-B Perception Model Transfer Evaluation
To evaluate sanding perception, the authors rendered 768 synthetic images across two workpiece types in 12 poses, covering unsanded, partially sanded, and completed states. These were split by workpiece pose into training (512), validation (128), and test (128) sets. Three configurations were compared:
1. SAM2 Baseline: Pretrained SAM2 without fine-tuning
2. Sim-only: Model fine-tuned purely on synthetic images
3. Sim + Real: Model trained on synthetic images plus labeled real images equal to roughly 20% of the synthetic set

Segmentation results on real test images for unsanded regions (TABLE II) were:
- Baseline: IoU 77.15%, Dice 86.97%, Precision 78.94%, Recall 97.34%
- Sim-only: IoU 84.47%, Dice 91.42%, Precision 91.18%, Recall 91.73%
- Sim + Real: IoU 97.41%, Dice 98.69%, Precision 98.62%, Recall 98.76%

Even the Sim-only model improved IoU by 7.32 points over baseline, with Precision jumping from 78.94% to 91.18%. Adding a small amount of real data reached an impressive 97.41% IoU, demonstrating strong practical utility.

captions.F4: Workpiece cross-section profiles after two grinding passes. The left shows optical scans, and the right plots cross-sections at $X = 20, 70, 120$ mm. Height changes show excellent agreement between real trials (dashed) and simulation (solid) as the bead apex flattens.
captions.F5: Segmentation results for unsanded regions (cyan masks) on real workpieces. Comparing (a) input image, (b) pretrained SAM2, (c) Sim-only, and (d) Sim + Real. Sim-only sharply reduces over-segmentation false positives, while adding real data in (d) captures exact boundaries.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: RoboFin3D offers a comprehensive sim-to-real platform reproducing physical dynamics and visual changes in grinding and sanding while connecting directly to perception training. Future work targets real-time contact solving, broader workpiece diversity, and pre-evaluating control policies.
sections.details:
This paper introduced RoboFin3D, a sim-to-real platform for robotic grinding and sanding. Combining SDFs and surface fields allows GPU-native handling of geometric and appearance changes without mesh extraction overhead. In addition, WeldGen supplies a large-scale welded workpiece dataset, and physical calibration confirms physical fidelity. The authors also demonstrated that synthetic data directly boosts perception model accuracy.

The authors highlight four areas for future research:
- Refining contact and removal models to match physical results even more closely
- Accelerating contact computations to achieve full real-time execution
- Quantifying sim-to-real gaps across more diverse workpiece shapes and process parameters
- Serving as an evaluation environment for grinding and sanding control policies (such as reinforcement learning) before real deployment

By allowing safe, repeatable trial-and-error in virtual space without destroying real workpieces, this platform is expected to accelerate research and development in robotic surface finishing.

takeaways: In simulations involving changing geometry, completing contact physics and rendering entirely via SDFs in shared GPU buffers without intermediate meshes is highly effective.
Decoupling large-scale geometric removal (grinding) from subtle surface finish shifts (sanding) across two separate representation layers—SDFs and surface fields—is an elegant architectural design.
Training purely on synthetic image data generated and annotated through physics-based simulation noticeably boosts real-image segmentation accuracy (+7.3 points in IoU).
limitations: Contact physics computation has not yet reached full real-time speed, requiring further acceleration.
Wear models and contact stiffness leave room for refinement, as simulated sanding overpredicted exposed area by 10% to 16% relative to physical experiments.
At this stage, policy training (e.g., reinforcement learning) within the simulator and its direct sim-to-real transfer remain unexplored and are left for future work.
